In Experiment 1, multiple RDKs at various difficulties (coherence levels) are presented for view and participants are instructed to correctly respond to as many of them as possible.

We tested 102 participants recruited through the Melbourne School of Psychological Sciences Research Experience Pool (Mean age = 19.24, age range = 17-40; 90 F, 12 M).
Participants were reimbursed with credit toward completion of a first year psychology subject.
Datasets from four subjects were excluded for completing the experiment twice (i.e., only the first of the datasets for these subjects was retained).
Fifty participants completed the experiment version where the location of task difficulty was Fixed.
In each condition, participants completed multiple trials in which they were asked to select and complete as many RDKs as possible.
On each trial, participants were shown a set of four labeled RDKs (see Figure 1).

Participants had to respond to the selected task as in Experiment 1.
We tested 105 participants recruited through the Melbourne School of Psychological Sciences Research Experience Pool (Mean age = 19.17, age range = 17-33, 81 F, 24 M).
Participants were reimbursed with credit toward completion of a first year psychology subject.

Five subjects were excluded from the Fixed condition and eight were removed from the Random condition for having less than chance accuracy on the easiest RDK leaving 46 participants in each condition.
One explanation is that participants are unable to tell apart the RDKs at the levels of coherence that we used.

Removing task completion left ample time to select all four tasks within the 6 second deadline, and the results indicated that participants were able to successfully order the RDKs when asked to do so.
In light of those results, the explanation is that participants are unable to tell apart the RDKs when there is limited time to do so.

Figure B1 shows that participants were able to do this accurately supporting the idea that reducing the time pressure (by removing task completions) allowed participants time to develop a more precise representation of difficulty.

We made two other changes to ensure that participants were incentivized to sample the RDK during selection.

For each observation window, participants completed 3 practice trials, which are not analyzed, 10 Long Deadline trials with a 30 second deadline, and 30 short deadline trials with a 3 second deadline.
The direction of the selected RDK was then resampled, and the participant had to respond with the direction of the selected RDK.
If an incorrect response was made, the task paused for 2.5 seconds, the direction was resampled, and the participant had to respond to the same RDK again.
Participants were not asked to produce free text or to answer questions whose content could be generated externally.

table.text: Sixty-one participants from the University of Melbourne were recruited through the undergraduate Research Experience Program and received subject credit in return for participation.

Datasets from 9 subjects were excluded for completing fewer than 20 deadline trials for completing the experiment more than once (i.e., only the first of the datasets for these subjects was retained) leaving 52 participants (43 Female, 9 Male, 1 Unspecified, age range 17-36).
Eighty-six participants were recruited in total (Bracketed (200|400|800) Condition N = 42, Anchored (400|800|1600) Condition N = 44).

Several participants were removed for completing less than 20 trials at any observation window leaving N = 34 in the Bracketed condition (29 F, 5 M; mean age 19, range 18-22) and N = 39 in the Anchored condition (32 F, 6 M, 1 Unspecified; mean age 19, range 18-24).
Participants were recruited from the Melbourne Research Experience Program and were reimbursed with credit toward an undergraduate psychology subject.
All participants completed the experiment in their own browser using an experiment programmed with JSPsych (De Leeuw, 2015).

> Participants had to respond to the selected task as in Experiment 1.

> We tested 105 participants recruited through the Melbourne School of Psychological Sciences Research Experience Pool (Mean age = 19.17, age range = 17-33, 81 F, 24 M).

> Five subjects were excluded from the Fixed condition and eight were removed from the Random condition for having less than chance accuracy on the easiest RDK leaving 46 participants in each condition.

> One explanation is that participants are unable to tell apart the RDKs at the levels of coherence that we used.

> Removing task completion left ample time to select all four tasks within the 6 second deadline, and the results indicated that participants were able to successfully order the RDKs when asked to do so.

> In light of those results, the explanation is that participants are unable to tell apart the RDKs when there is limited time to do so.

> Figure B1 shows that participants were able to do this accurately supporting the idea that reducing the time pressure (by removing task completions) allowed participants time to develop a more precise representation of difficulty.

> After selection, that RDK direction was resampled and the participant had to respond with the RDK direction (until correct as in Experiments 1 and 2), before being returned to the selection screen.

> We made two other changes to ensure that participants were incentivized to sample the RDK during selection.

> For each observation window, participants completed 3 practice trials, which are not analyzed, 10 Long Deadline trials with a 30 second deadline, and 30 short deadline trials with a 3 second deadline.

> The direction of the selected RDK was then resampled, and the participant had to respond with the direction of the selected RDK.

> If an incorrect response was made, the task paused for 2.5 seconds, the direction was resampled, and the participant had to respond to the same RDK again.

> Participants were not asked to produce free text or to answer questions whose content could be generated externally.

> Participants were recruited through university research participation schemes rather than open online marketplaces, and were reimbursed with course credit rather than payment, which further reduces the incentive for automated participation.

> Our participants were young, predominantly female undergraduate students.

> Participants were able to order the tasks from easiest to hardest when there was ample time to do so (see Figure B1.

> Sixty-one participants from the University of Melbourne were recruited through the undergraduate Research Experience Program and received subject credit in return for participation.

> Datasets from 9 subjects were excluded for completing fewer than 20 deadline trials for completing the experiment more than once (i.e., only the first of the datasets for these subjects was retained) leaving 52 participants (43 Female, 9 Male, 1 Unspecified, age range 17-36).

> Participants were recruited from the Melbourne Research Experience Program and were reimbursed with credit toward an undergraduate psychology subject.

> All participants completed the experiment in their own browser using an experiment programmed with JSPsych (De Leeuw, 2015).

power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: Power analysis for a chi-square test of uniformity, used for analyzing the selection orders, indicated that an N of 47 provides 95% power for detecting a difference from random responding. We aimed to collect at least 45 participants in each condition or as many as the testing period would allow. The experiment was programmed in HTML and Javascript using the jsPsych package (De Leeuw, 2015) and administered over the participant's browser. Human Research Participant was approved by the University of Melbourne Human Research Ethics Committee (ID 2056156.3). Data for Experiment 1 were collected in 2020.

After the integration window, all of the displays stopped moving until a selection was made; thus difficulty can only be judged during the integration window. Selection can be made at any time, either during the integration window or after the RDKs have stopped moving. After selection, that RDK direction was resampled and the participant had to respond with the RDK direction (until correct as in Experiments 1 and 2), before being returned to the selection screen. We made two other changes to ensure that participants were incentivized to sample the RDK during selection. First, the deadline was decreased from 6 seconds to 3 seconds, and second, the penalty for an incorrect RDK response was increased to from .5 s to 2 s. Both of these manipulations work to offset the cost of sampling by increasing the amount by which an SPT strategy allows a greater number of task completions over a random strategy. That is, should a difficult task be selected first, the penalty for guessing incorrectly would take out over half of the remaining time. We expect the distance from an SPT optimal strategy should decrease as the observation window increases allowing for a better representation of task difficulty. To estimate the number of participants needed in each condition, we consider that the standard deviation of difficulty scales as σ(T ) = σ ref (T ref /T ) because noise accumulates with (t) (Gold & Shadlen, 2007; Ratcliff, 1978). σ ref was set to .57 and T ref = 1455 ms (see Appendix B). At 200, 400, 800, and 1600 ms, this gives values of σ of 1.54, 1.09, 0.77, and 0.54. The strict deadline in Experiment 3, coupled with a more severe time penalty, means that the number of tasks completed may be severely truncated. Consequently, we focus on P (Easiest First). Assuming a deterministic easiest-first policy gives P (Easiest First) predictions of .36, .41, .48, and .56, which we use as effect sizes to determine the sample size. At 30 trials per T obs and moderate between-subject variability, power for a positive linear trend exceeded .99 at N = 30. We for both outcome measures and both sets of levels; a target of N = 30-40 was adopted.

prereg_check.title: Preregistration Check

table.title: Human Scheduling of Perceptual Tasks
table.research_questions:
The optimal policy to minimize the number of tasks completed after the deadline (or i.e., to maximize the number of tasks completed before the deadline) is to complete shortest subtask first. 

We will determine whether participants converge to this optimal schedule. We will compare scheduling both with and without a deadline and expect greater optimality when participants have to complete the RDK task under a deadline. 

We expect greater optimality when difficulty location is held constant compared to when it is varied from trial to trial.
table.study_type: Experiment - A researcher randomly assigns treatments to study subjects, this includes field or lab experiments. This is also known as an intervention experiment and includes randomized controlled trials.
table.blinding: No blinding is involved in this study.
table.randomization: Location of RDKs (i.e., RDK difficulty) will be randomized across participants. RDK direction and instantiation is randomized from selection to selection. RDK coherence is held constant across trials.
table.existing_data: Registration prior to creation of data
table.sample_size:
We will recruit 50 participants.

Each participant will complete 10 no deadline scheduling trials and 30 deadline scheduling trials via a web browser.
table.sample_size_rationale: This is a preliminary study. Sample size is chosen based on pragmatic considerations.
table.stopping_rule: Sampling will be stopped after 50 participants have been collected in each condition.
table.manipulated_variables: We will manipulate the coherence and direction of four RDK tasks and the deadline available for selection and completion of the four tasks on each trial. We will additionally manipulate whether there was a deadline or not. 5ea634c43854e200ce6a55fe prereg.pdf https://osf.io/project/pcjsb/files/osfstorage/5ea634c43854e200ce6a55fe https://osf.io/download/5ea634c43854e200ce6a55fe b165d28231cab41a0615fcc4bbea2cf447a520d96d15d118d8a51f9641e58927
table.measured_variables: The main variable is the order in which subtasks are completed. Secondary variables are the accuracy and completion time of the RDK subtasks. 5ea634c43854e200ce6a55fe prereg.pdf https://osf.io/project/pcjsb/files/osfstorage/5ea634c43854e200ce6a55fe https://osf.io/download/5ea634c43854e200ce6a55fe b165d28231cab41a0615fcc4bbea2cf447a520d96d15d118d8a51f9641e58927
table.statistical_tests:
For each participant, the optimal order of each location will be determined (i.e., from easiest to hardest). The first analysis will compute something like Kendall's Tau, rank-order distance. What we want is the distance of the selected options from the optimal solutions, which is Kendall's Tau. However, because a participant may run out of time, there may be missing values. To handle these values, for each trial, we find the orders which partially match the selected order and compute: (1) the maximum distance of those possible orders and the optimal solution and (2) the average distance of those possible orders and the optimal solution. 

We will examine the distribution of distances across participants to determine how much they deviate from optimal. Bayesian analysis will be used to characterise the posterior uncertainty in distance across trials.

We will perform a similar analysis using the proportion of first-optimal responses (i.e., the proportion of responses in which the first chosen option is the easiest).

We will additionally create "spatial-order" strategies (e.g., clockwise strategy, anti-clockwise strategy) and compute the partial-matching Kendall's Tau measure of the response to these spatial orders. These strategies may be non-optimal, depending on the random distribution of difficulties; nonetheless, participants may adopt these strategies.

For completeness, we will additionally analyse the completion time and accuracy of the RDK task to ensure that coherence mapped to difficulty and average completion time the expected manner.

We will compare the optimality of the first 10 untimed trials against the first 10 deadline trials and the last 10 deadline trials using a Bayesian one-way ANOVA and a hierarchical Bayesian model described below. 5ea634c43854e200ce6a55fe prereg.pdf https://osf.io/project/pcjsb/files/osfstorage/5ea634c43854e200ce6a55fe https://osf.io/download/5ea634c43854e200ce6a55fe b165d28231cab41a0615fcc4bbea2cf447a520d96d15d118d8a51f9641e58927
table.inference_criteria: Posterior parameter estimation will be used for inference. Optimality (measured using normalised Kendall's Tau adjusted for missing data as described above) will be given a uniform Beta(1,1) prior in each condition. We will compare two models, one in which the hyperpriors are free to vary across the untimed, deadline (first 10), and deadline (last 10) conditions, and one in which the hyperpriors are fixed. Posterior parameter estimation and DIC will be used to examine whether there is a credible difference in optimality between deadline conditions.
table.data_exclusion_criteria: Participants will be excluded if they do not complete all trials. Initial analysis of complete participant data will not exclude any data. Followup analyses may exclude data on the basis of RDK completion time.
table.missing_data_handling: Participants will be excluded if they do not complete all trials.
table.exploratory_analyses: Most of the data analyses considered so far may be considered exploratory in that we make no particular hypothesis as to whether scheduling should be optimal or not.

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list("P-Value" = c("p's > .05", "p < .05", "p < .05", 
"p < .05"), Text = c("However, the main effect of condition and all other interactions were not significant (p's > .05).", 
"The deadline did result in significantly fewer tasks being completed (Wilcox V = 125, p < .05).", 
"Both are different from uniform random responding (Untimed: χ 2 (3) = 48.5, p < .05, W = .31;", 
"Deadline: χ 2 (3) = 37.7, p < .05, W = .24).")), row.names = c(NA, 
-4L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame"))

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 2, FALSE)
```

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. ethics_statements: Human Research Participant was approved by the University of Melbourne Human Research Ethics Committee (ID 2056156.3).
Data for Experiment 2 were collected in 2021 under the same ethics approval as Experiment 1.
live_data_statements: Using a task initially developed by Sheridan and Tulga (1978), participants were shown a series of moving rectangles that progressed toward a short vertical bar (e.g., the deadline) over the course of about 30 seconds.
When only deadline or duration varied, participants completed the tasks optimally (i.e., either closest deadline first or shortest width first, respectively, at least in the easiest conditions).
In Experiment 1, multiple RDKs at various difficulties (coherence levels) are presented for view and participants are instructed to correctly respond to as many of them as possible.
Consequently, if participants are sensitive to the optimal scheduling order (cf. Moray et al., 1991), then scheduling prioritization should approach an SPT policy.
Because task difficulty is estimated with lower precision, even if participants are sensitive to the optimal order, scheduling may deviate from an SPT policy.
We tested 102 participants recruited through the Melbourne School of Psychological Sciences Research Experience Pool (Mean age = 19.24, age range = 17-40; 90 F, 12 M).
Participants were reimbursed with credit toward completion of a first year psychology subject.
Datasets from four subjects were excluded for completing the experiment twice (i.e., only the first of the datasets for these subjects was retained).
Fifty participants completed the experiment version where the location of task difficulty was Fixed.
In each condition, participants completed multiple trials in which they were asked to select and complete as many RDKs as possible.
On each trial, participants were shown a set of four labeled RDKs (see Figure 1).

Participants completed the experiment by clicking a link with a uniquely generated ID code; the link could have been used multiple times, and participants were able to exit the experiment at any time.
Participants had to respond to the selected task as in Experiment 1.
We tested 105 participants recruited through the Melbourne School of Psychological Sciences Research Experience Pool (Mean age = 19.17, age range = 17-33, 81 F, 24 M).

Five subjects were excluded from the Fixed condition and eight were removed from the Random condition for having less than chance accuracy on the easiest RDK leaving 46 participants in each condition.
One explanation is that participants are unable to tell apart the RDKs at the levels of coherence that we used.

Removing task completion left ample time to select all four tasks within the 6 second deadline, and the results indicated that participants were able to successfully order the RDKs when asked to do so.
In light of those results, the explanation is that participants are unable to tell apart the RDKs when there is limited time to do so.

Figure B1 shows that participants were able to do this accurately supporting the idea that reducing the time pressure (by removing task completions) allowed participants time to develop a more precise representation of difficulty.
After selection, that RDK direction was resampled and the participant had to respond with the RDK direction (until correct as in Experiments 1 and 2), before being returned to the selection screen.
We made two other changes to ensure that participants were incentivized to sample the RDK during selection.

For each observation window, participants completed 3 practice trials, which are not analyzed, 10 Long Deadline trials with a 30 second deadline, and 30 short deadline trials with a 3 second deadline.
The direction of the selected RDK was then resampled, and the participant had to respond with the direction of the selected RDK.
If an incorrect response was made, the task paused for 2.5 seconds, the direction was resampled, and the participant had to respond to the same RDK again.
Participants were not asked to produce free text or to answer questions whose content could be generated externally.

Participants were recruited through university research participation schemes rather than open online marketplaces, and were reimbursed with course credit rather than payment, which further reduces the incentive for automated participation.
that a ranking model will fit this data well since this task varies considerably from a standard preference ranking in that participants were required to complete each task after selecting it.
Our participants were young, predominantly female undergraduate students.

The design, procedure, and data analysis steps were analogous to Experiment 2, with the exception that participants were only required to click on each RDK and were instructed to select RDKs in order of easiest to hardest.
Participants were able to order the tasks from easiest to hardest when there was ample time to do so (see Figure B1.
Sixty-one participants from the University of Melbourne were recruited through the undergraduate Research Experience Program and received subject credit in return for participation.

Datasets from 9 subjects were excluded for completing fewer than 20 deadline trials for completing the experiment more than once (i.e., only the first of the datasets for these subjects was retained) leaving 52 participants (43 Female, 9 Male, 1 Unspecified, age range 17-36).
Eighty-six participants were recruited in total (Bracketed (200|400|800) Condition N = 42, Anchored (400|800|1600) Condition N = 44).

Several participants were removed for completing less than 20 trials at any observation window leaving N = 34 in the Bracketed condition (29 F, 5 M; mean age 19, range 18-22) and N = 39 in the Anchored condition (32 F, 6 M, 1 Unspecified; mean age 19, range 18-24).
Participants were recruited from the Melbourne Research Experience Program and were reimbursed with credit toward an undergraduate psychology subject.
All participants completed the experiment in their own browser using an experiment programmed with JSPsych (De Leeuw, 2015).

results show that good prioritization depends on how clearly task difficulty can be seen or communicated.
This matters for the design of workplaces, software interfaces, and instructions in settings such as healthcare, education, and transport, where people juggle competing tasks under deadlines.
Many tasks and decisions are multi-component, requiring the application of limited capacity cognitive resources to extract, process, and integrate information.

For example, a doctor diagnosing a patient or a defense operator making a risk assessment may consider and combine various diagnostic measurements and symptoms or signals; a scientist researching a topic has to contend with a broad literature containing articles of varying relevance and quality; an investor considering financial options has to consider advice which is often noisy at best and fraudulent at worst.
Scheduling priorities may be non-optimal and inefficient due to a failure to apply an optimal policy.
Alternatively, scheduling might fail because the representation of the inputs to that policy is uncertain and variable.

Scheduling theory was developed in operations engineering, to manage workflow across limited machines, and in software engineering, to manage allocation of resources (e.g., RAM) across limited processors (Bellman, 1956; French, 1982; Robert & Vivien, 2009; W. E. Smith, 1956).
text.formatted: Scheduling theory was developed in operations engineering, to manage workflow across limited machines, and in software engineering, to manage allocation of resources (e.g., RAM) across limited processors <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Bellman, 1956;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">French, 1982;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b103">Robert & Vivien, 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b120">W. E. Smith, 1956)</ref>.

text.text: Scheduling theory specifies that for any multi-component problem, the critical determinants of the optimal policy are the effort or difficulty required by each sub-component, the rewards or costs afforded by each sub-component, and the overall goal (e.g., maximizing reward, completing as many tasks as possible before a deadline, minimizing task lateness, maximizing reward rate, to name a few).

Classical scheduling theory assumes that these factors are known (exactly in the case of deterministic scheduling and at the distributional level for probabilistic scheduling, Bellman, 1956; French, 1982; McKay & Wiers, 1999; Pinedo, 1983).
text.formatted: Classical scheduling theory assumes that these factors are known (exactly in the case of deterministic scheduling and at the distributional level for probabilistic scheduling, <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Bellman, 1956;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">French, 1982;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b77">McKay & Wiers, 1999;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b88">Pinedo, 1983)</ref>.

text.text: Rapid prioritization decisions, however, must often be made at a glance, drawing on perceptual information and prior knowledge to classify and order subsequent tasks and information.
In the present paper, we compare performance of a single observer as they complete up to four tasks that vary in difficulty across multiple trials.

We start by briefly reviewing scheduling theory in order to show its relevance to broader psychological and cognitive questions and to develop the optimal scheduling order in the constrained setting that we explore in this paper.
Scheduling theory provides a rich analysis of different contexts and constraints; the optimal scheduling order is sensitive to those factors.
Consequently, we make clear at the outset, how the benchmark optimal order (i.e., a shortest-processing time first order) is derived.

Initial theoretical treatment of a general scheduling problem was presented by Bellman (1956), though special cases of scheduling problems, relevant to the present paper, were discussed prior to this (W. E. Smith, 1956).
text.formatted: Initial theoretical treatment of a general scheduling problem was presented by <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Bellman (1956)</ref>, though special cases of scheduling problems, relevant to the present paper, were discussed prior to this (W. E. <ref type="bibr" target="#b120">Smith, 1956)</ref>.

text.text: Scheduling theory uses a four parameter classification of job shop problems in the following format: n/m/A/B (Conway, Maxwell, & Miller, 1967). 1 n is a scalar value that refers to the number of jobs or tasks to complete. m is also a scalar that refers to the number of machines or operators.
text.formatted: Scheduling theory uses a four parameter classification of job shop problems in the following format: n/m/A/B <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Conway, Maxwell, & Miller, 1967</ref>). 1 n is a scalar value that refers to the number of jobs or tasks to complete. m is also a scalar that refers to the number of machines or operators.

text.text: A describes any restrictions on the problem (further detailed below).
B specifies the performance measure or goal.
In the present paper, we restrict the number of tasks to n = 4 and concern ourselves with the case where there is a single operator who can complete one task at a time, m = 1.
The choice of four tasks allows examination of a sufficiently large number of possible orders allowing us to determine what characteristics affect optimal prioritization.
A is an index that specifies a number of restrictions on the scheduling problem; for instance, some tasks might be available only after completing another task (i.e., task contingency).
Another factor indexed by A is whether preemption is permitted; that is, once a task has started does it need to be processed to completion?
Or can processing be interrupted and a different task selected?

When preemption is permitted, scheduling problems are analogous to foraging problems; that is, processing of a source (or exploitation of a patch) should be maintained until the expected value of the source drops below some value (Charnov, 1976).
text.formatted: When preemption is permitted, scheduling problems are analogous to foraging problems; that is, processing of a source (or exploitation of a patch) should be maintained until the expected value of the source drops below some value <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Charnov, 1976)</ref>.

text.text: Such effects are often found in the dynamics of multiple goal completions tasks (e.g., Ballard, Farrell, & Neal, 2018a; Ballard et al., 2022; Ballard, Vancouver, & Neal, 2018; Ballard, Yeo, Loft, Vancouver, & Neal, 2016; Ballard, Yeo, Neal, & Farrell, 2016; Hotaling, 2020; Neal, Ballard, & Vancouver, 2017;  1 Other problem classification systems are also used that involve fewer or more parameters depending on the problem class (cf., Graham, Lawler, Lenstra, & Kan, 1979). Schmidt & DeShon, 2007; Vancouver, Weinhardt, & Schmidt, 2010).
text.formatted: Such effects are often found in the dynamics of multiple goal completions tasks (e.g., <ref type="bibr">Ballard, Farrell, & Neal, 2018a;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Ballard et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Ballard, Vancouver, & Neal, 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">Ballard, Yeo, Loft, Vancouver, & Neal, 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Ballard, Yeo, Neal, & Farrell, 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">Hotaling, 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b83">Neal, Ballard, & Vancouver, 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr"/> 1 Other problem classification systems are also used that involve fewer or more parameters depending on the problem class (cf., <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">Graham, Lawler, Lenstra, & Kan, 1979)</ref>. <ref type="bibr" target="#b106">Schmidt & DeShon, 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b130">Vancouver, Weinhardt, & Schmidt, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: For simplicity, in the present paper, we address tasks without contingency or preemption, setting those questions aside for future investigation.

Regardless of whether contingencies are preserved or preemption is allowed, the primary determinant of the optimal policy is the goal, B. Some relevant examples of goals are completing as many tasks as possible before some deadline, maximizing reward, or minimizing the maximum lateness of any task.
Under conditions where the duration of each task is known (i.e., deterministic scheduling), optimal solutions can be generated for these types of problems.

For example, if deadlines vary between tasks, then to minimize the maximum lateness of any task, tasks should be completed in order of deadline (known as earliest due date scheduling; W. E. Smith, 1956).
text.formatted: For example, if deadlines vary between tasks, then to minimize the maximum lateness of any task, tasks should be completed in order of deadline (known as earliest due date scheduling; W. E. <ref type="bibr" target="#b120">Smith, 1956)</ref>.

text.text: If all tasks share a common deadline, then to minimize the maximum lateness of any tasks, tasks should be completed in order of shortest-to-longest completion time (i.e., Shortest Processing Time first or SPT).
This is equivalent to minimizing the maximum wait time of any task and also equivalent to minimizing the total sum of completion times (French, 1982; W. E. Smith, 1956).
text.formatted: This is equivalent to minimizing the maximum wait time of any task and also equivalent to minimizing the total sum of completion times <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(French, 1982;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b120">W. E. Smith, 1956)</ref>.

text.text: When rewards are equivalent (meaning that equal rewards accompany the completion of each task), scheduling based on the reward rate also favors a shortest-to-longest (SPT) completion schedule.
Note that this optimal order is not obvious, and popular advice often recommends tackling the most difficult tasks first without regard for optimality (e.g., Levitin, 2014).
text.formatted: Note that this optimal order is not obvious, and popular advice often recommends tackling the most difficult tasks first without regard for optimality (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">Levitin, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: With these constraints, the scheduling classification would be the case where there are n = 4 tasks to complete, m = 1 operator, no preemption, -P , no contingency, -C, and the goal is to complete as many tasks as possible before a deadline; hence, an n = 4/m = 1/A = {-P, -C}/B = {maximize number of tasks completed} problem.

In the case where the n tasks have different completion times but constant reward/cost, this problem captures the prioritization elements of a number of decision making questions across a large array of paradigms, both basic and applied, such as the following: searching n targets in a visual search display, categorizing multidimensional stimuli where each of n features is relevant, detection of targets in a redundant target display, problem solving with multiple steps, memory retrieval, medical diagnosis, and information search (e.g., deciding which links to click from a set of hyperlinks) among others.
The specific n/m/A/B problem adopted here forms a tractable starting point for considering the efficiency of human scheduling performance.
Determining the optimal policy depends on knowing, at least approximately, the distribution of task finishing-times, rewards, and the goal state (McKay & Wiers, 1999).
text.formatted: Determining the optimal policy depends on knowing, at least approximately, the distribution of task finishing-times, rewards, and the goal state <ref type="bibr" target="#b77">(McKay & Wiers, 1999)</ref>.

text.text: This requires either sufficient experience with each task such that input parameters can be estimated precisely, or some indication of the difficulty or average completion time.

For instance, in a single machine job problem with multiple tasks to complete, if tasks differ in value, then we can assign each task a weight according to its importance divided by the time to complete, and then complete tasks in order of decreasing ratio (W. E. Smith, 1956).
text.formatted: For instance, in a single machine job problem with multiple tasks to complete, if tasks differ in value, then we can assign each task a weight according to its importance divided by the time to complete, and then complete tasks in order of decreasing ratio (W. E. <ref type="bibr" target="#b120">Smith, 1956)</ref>.

text.text: This example of a dynamic allocation index, known as "Smith's rule", provides a near-optimal completion order policy in many general situations.
Intuitively, the policy reveals that tasks that take twice as long to complete need to be twice as important to be given priority.

A general solution to more complex scheduling problems (along with many other problems classed as Markov decision processes, MDP's; Gittins, Glazebrook, & Weber, 2011) in the form of a dynamic allocation index was provided by Gittins (1974) and Gittins and Jones (1979).
text.formatted: A general solution to more complex scheduling problems (along with many other problems classed as Markov decision processes, MDP's; <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">Gittins, Glazebrook, & Weber, 2011)</ref> in the form of a dynamic allocation index was provided by <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Gittins (1974)</ref> and <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">Gittins and Jones (1979)</ref>.

text.text: In the Appendix, we show that applying the Gittins Index to the present case results in selection orders which correspond to the scheduling theory orders in many cases, including the present experiments.

That a general Gittins index policy applies to scheduling implies a strong link between questions of scheduling and multi-armed bandit problems (e.g., where the observer must choose between several possible gambles each with different payoffs or costs; M. D. Lee, Zhang, Munro, & Steyvers, 2011; Robbins, 1952; Sutton & Barto, 1998), questions of exploration/exploitation (Cogliati, Cleeremans, & Alexander, 2019; Gonzalez & Dutt, 2011; Lejarraga, Dutt, & Gonzalez, 2012; Mehlhorn et al., 2015; Wilson, Geana, White, Ludvig, & Cohen, 2014), and foraging (Pirolli, 2007; Pirolli & Card, 1999).
text.formatted: That a general Gittins index policy applies to scheduling implies a strong link between questions of scheduling and multi-armed bandit problems (e.g., where the observer must choose between several possible gambles each with different payoffs or costs; M. D. <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">Lee, Zhang, Munro, & Steyvers, 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b102">Robbins, 1952;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b121">Sutton & Barto, 1998)</ref>, questions of exploration/exploitation <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Cogliati, Cleeremans, & Alexander, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Gonzalez & Dutt, 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">Lejarraga, Dutt, & Gonzalez, 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b78">Mehlhorn et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b142">Wilson, Geana, White, Ludvig, & Cohen, 2014)</ref>, and foraging <ref type="bibr" target="#b89">(Pirolli, 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b90">Pirolli & Card, 1999)</ref>.

text.text: In many scheduling tasks, only some components of the problem are readily available.
For instance, one might be aware of the remaining to-be-completed tasks, the amount of time available to complete them, and perhaps roughly how important or valuable each task is.

Other parameters, important for determining the optimal scheduling order, like the difficulty, duration, or effort involved to complete a task are latent parameters that must be inferred from cues or prior experience.
It is useful to frame this problem as a Markov decision problem with mixed observability (a MOMDP).
A MOMDP is a class of partially-observable MDP (a POMDP; Astrom, 1965; Smallwood & Sondik, 1973).
text.formatted: A MOMDP is a class of partially-observable MDP (a POMDP; <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">Astrom, 1965;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b115">Smallwood & Sondik, 1973)</ref>.

text.text: Both frameworks pose the decision problem as an interaction between the observer and the environment (Littman, 2009) and in both, contra to a standard MDP, the state of the world must be inferred through observation or through sampling information.
text.formatted: Both frameworks pose the decision problem as an interaction between the observer and the environment <ref type="bibr" target="#b68">(Littman, 2009)</ref> and in both, contra to a standard MDP, the state of the world must be inferred through observation or through sampling information.

text.text: The main distinction is that in a MOMDP, some information (e.g., number of tasks, time remaining) is known while other information (e.g., duration and effort of each task) is not.

Briefly, the key components of the framework are a set of states that an observer or agent transitions through by taking actions (in accord with the probability of transitioning from one state to the next; Littman, 2009).
text.formatted: Briefly, the key components of the framework are a set of states that an observer or agent transitions through by taking actions (in accord with the probability of transitioning from one state to the next; <ref type="bibr" target="#b68">Littman, 2009)</ref>.

text.text: Information about states is gathered through observation and updated (using Bayes rule) across learning, and a control policy is learned through reinforcement to optimize reward across actions and states (Rao, 2010).
text.formatted: Information about states is gathered through observation and updated (using Bayes rule) across learning, and a control policy is learned through reinforcement to optimize reward across actions and states <ref type="bibr" target="#b97">(Rao, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: Of interest to the current investigation is how scheduling policies depend on the precision of the observations.

If the state is uncertain (e.g., is the current task difficult or easy?) because of an imprecise representation, then the scheduling policy (even if known exactly) may become sub-optimal in execution.

On the other hand, if an optimal scheduling policy is unknown or in error, then known task properties might lead to sub-optimal prioritization (e.g., completing the difficult task first to get it out of the way).

In one of the few psychology studies examining how human performance compares to scheduling theory benchmarks, Moray, Dessouky, Kijowski, and Adapathya (1991) tested how participants prioritize the completion of multiple tasks under time pressure using scheduling theory as a normative comparison.
text.formatted: In one of the few psychology studies examining how human performance compares to scheduling theory benchmarks, <ref type="bibr" target="#b81">Moray, Dessouky, Kijowski, and Adapathya (1991)</ref> tested how participants prioritize the completion of multiple tasks under time pressure using scheduling theory as a normative comparison.

text.text: Using a task initially developed by Sheridan and Tulga (1978), participants were shown a series of moving rectangles that progressed toward a short vertical bar (e.g., the deadline) over the course of about 30 seconds.
text.formatted: Using a task initially developed by <ref type="bibr" target="#b111">Sheridan and Tulga (1978)</ref>, participants were shown a series of moving rectangles that progressed toward a short vertical bar (e.g., the deadline) over the course of about 30 seconds.

text.text: The width of the rectangle could be decreased (representing effort on task or task processing) by placing the mouse cursor over the rectangle.
Participants could switch rectangles at any time, but only the selected rectangle would decrease in width.
The goal was to reduce as many rectangles as possible to zero width before they reached their respective deadlines, under conditions where deadline, task duration, or both varied.
When only deadline or duration varied, participants completed the tasks optimally (i.e., either closest deadline first or shortest width first, respectively, at least in the easiest conditions).
However, this was not the case when both varied.
As time pressure increased, subjective workload also increased, and performance (measured by the number of completed rectangles) decreased.

Participants also often failed to follow the optimal rule directly, even when explicitly told in advance; knowing the rule also increased subjective workload when the rule was complex to the extent that no participant was able to successfully complete the task when the rule was explicit but both deadline and duration varied.
The nature of the Moray et al. (1991) task does not lend itself to easy comparison with other cognitive tasks both in and outside of the lab.
text.formatted: The nature of the <ref type="bibr" target="#b81">Moray et al. (1991)</ref> task does not lend itself to easy comparison with other cognitive tasks both in and outside of the lab.

text.text: For one, "processing" involved no work (cognitive or otherwise) aside from placing a mouse cursor in the correct position.
In everyday scheduling, once a task is selected for processing, some cognitive or physical effort is then required to complete the task (see e.g., Wickens, Gutzwiller, & Santamaria, 2015).
text.formatted: In everyday scheduling, once a task is selected for processing, some cognitive or physical effort is then required to complete the task (see e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b136">Wickens, Gutzwiller, & Santamaria, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: The shift in context from scheduling to processing may incur some cost that is critical, yet unexplored in Moray et al.'s study (Rogers & Monsell, 1995).
text.formatted: The shift in context from scheduling to processing may incur some cost that is critical, yet unexplored in Moray et al.'s study <ref type="bibr" target="#b104">(Rogers & Monsell, 1995)</ref>.

text.text: Two, in Moray et al.'s task, difficulty (e.g., rectangle length) and amount of time to deadline were known and easily comparable to each other (i.e., it's easy to judge whether or not the rectangle width was less than the distance to the deadline by comparing two line lengths).
Consequently, Moray et al.'s results cannot speak to whether the precision of observations has a downstream impact on scheduling optimality.
In the current paper, task completion durations varied across experiments.
We also varied how easy or difficult it was to determine the effort required to complete a task.
To foreshadow, this latter manipulation had significant implications for whether or not participants scheduled tasks optimally.
Our paradigm introduces trials in which multiple tasks are presented that can only be attempted one at a time.
Tasks are forced to be completed sequentially so we can focus on the choice of which task to complete at each scheduling or task selection stage.
We additionally require that the duration of each task can be controlled so that the tasks may be ordered in their difficulty (at the distribution level).
For a variety of reasons, random dot kinematograms (RDKs) are useful for this purpose.
In an RDK, dots move left or right randomly within an aperture with some proportion of dots moving coherently either to the left or the right.

The RDK was initially developed to examine how the individual motion of the dots is aggregated by the motion system to give a perception of coherent global motion without relevant displacement signals (Baker Jr & Braddick, 1982; Van de Grind, Van Doorn, & Koenderink, 1983).
text.formatted: The RDK was initially developed to examine how the individual motion of the dots is aggregated by the motion system to give a perception of coherent global motion without relevant displacement signals <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Baker Jr & Braddick, 1982;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b131">Van de Grind, Van Doorn, & Koenderink, 1983)</ref>.

text.text: Later studies of decision making used the RDK extensively to examine the dynamics of choice decision making in both humans (Palmer, Huk, & Shadlen, 2005) and non-human primates (Shadlen & Newsome, 2001).
text.formatted: Later studies of decision making used the RDK extensively to examine the dynamics of choice decision making in both humans <ref type="bibr" target="#b85">(Palmer, Huk, & Shadlen, 2005)</ref> and non-human primates <ref type="bibr" target="#b110">(Shadlen & Newsome, 2001)</ref>.

text.text: The primary benefit of using the RDK for studying scheduling behavior, our purposes, is that we control the difficulty of motion-direction judgment by manipulating coherence and ultimately affect the response time for making that decision (Ludwig & Evens, 2017).
text.formatted: The primary benefit of using the RDK for studying scheduling behavior, our purposes, is that we control the difficulty of motion-direction judgment by manipulating coherence and ultimately affect the response time for making that decision <ref type="bibr" target="#b74">(Ludwig & Evens, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: In Experiment 1, multiple RDKs at various difficulties (coherence levels) are presented for view and participants are instructed to correctly respond to as many of them as possible.

They can only select one RDK at a time, so there is need to determine, at each point in time, which RDK to attempt next (i. e., schedule the order of which task to completion); we examine scheduling when difficulty is labeled and can therefore be estimated with high precision.
Consequently, if participants are sensitive to the optimal scheduling order (cf. Moray et al., 1991), then scheduling prioritization should approach an SPT policy.
text.formatted: Consequently, if participants are sensitive to the optimal scheduling order (cf. <ref type="bibr" target="#b81">Moray et al., 1991)</ref>, then scheduling prioritization should approach an SPT policy.

text.text: In Experiment 2, difficulty is not explicit but rather indicated by the dynamic motion of the RDK task during the selection stage.
Direction is resampled after task selection so the information from the selection stage only informs the magnitude of the coherent motion but not its sign.
We limit the total amount of time available to complete all of the tasks so that developing a precise estimate of coherence is costly and depletes the overall time available for completing the task.
Because task difficulty is estimated with lower precision, even if participants are sensitive to the optimal order, scheduling may deviate from an SPT policy.
In our experiments, on each trial, four RDK tasks of varied difficulty (i.e., coherence) are presented to the participant (see Figure 1).
text.formatted: In our experiments, on each trial, four RDK tasks of varied difficulty (i.e., coherence) are presented to the participant (see Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">1</ref>).

text.text: Participants must then select, one by one, in the order in which they wish to complete the RDKs (e.g., from easy to hardest, hard to easy, etc).
The RDK selected first is then presented for a direction judgment until the direction is identified correctly.
If the response is incorrect, then the direction is resampled (a time penalty is also added), and the participant must respond again (until the RDK direction judgment is correct).
Following the correct completion of the first RDK judgment, the participant is returned to the selection screen but now with the completed option removed.
The selection and completion of RDKs continues either until all available time has elapsed or until all four tasks have been completed.
We focus our analysis on the order in which RDKs are selected for completion both with and without the pressure of a deadline on performance.
In the present application, all tasks have equivalent rewards and deadlines.
Hence, since only difficulty (or completion time) varies between tasks, the optimal order is to complete the RDKs from shortest to longest decision time (i.e., SPT).

In the first experiment, the difficulty of each RDK was indicated explicitly by a text label ("Easy", "Medium", "Hard", or "Very Hard") that corresponded to the coherence of the RDK, as shown in Figure 1.
text.formatted: In the first experiment, the difficulty of each RDK was indicated explicitly by a text label ("Easy", "Medium", "Hard", or "Very Hard") that corresponded to the coherence of the RDK, as shown in Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">1</ref>.

text.text: In many contexts, task difficulty is unknown or must be learned from experience, but there are often cues from which difficulty can be rapidly assessed.
When faced with a set of articles to read, the length of an article can be used to estimate the reading time; such an estimate would require amount of processing time to determine.
Some websites provide an explicit estimate of reading time at the outset of an article.
The first example represents an unlabeled difficulty task, while the second provides an example of a labeled difficulty task.
The observed precision of the latent representation depends on the quality of the cue and on the processing time allocated to processing that cue.

In the Fixed Location condition of Experiment 1 the difficulty was allocated to the same location on each trial (but randomly varied across subjects) whereas in another Random Location condition, difficulty in each location varied randomly from trial to trial.
In the Random Location condition, trial-by-trial learning effects are attenuated allowing the representation of difficulty to be developed only through sampling, which takes time.
In the Fixed Location condition, across trials, the learned location-to-difficulty mapping will accumulate across trials so precision should be higher under a Fixed Location.

We additionally tested two phases: an Untimed phase, where there was ample time on each trial to complete all four RDKs, and a Deadline phase, where a fixed amount of time was allocated that was only sufficient to complete about three of the four RDKs.
In the Untimed phase, any order is sufficient to complete all of the tasks; consequently, prioritization order in this phase provides an indication of policy bias (i.e., toward a particular order).
Under a deadline, the optimal order will allow more tasks to be completed than than a non-optimal order putting pressure on the scheduling policy to improve performance.
Neither reward nor deadline were varied between tasks.
Participants & Apparatus.
text.formatted: Participants & Apparatus.

text.text: We tested 102 participants recruited through the Melbourne School of Psychological Sciences Research Experience Pool (Mean age = 19.24, age range = 17-40; 90 F, 12 M).
Participants were reimbursed with credit toward completion of a first year psychology subject.
Datasets from four subjects were excluded for completing the experiment twice (i.e., only the first of the datasets for these subjects was retained).
Fifty participants completed the experiment version where the location of task difficulty was Fixed.
In this condition, the locations of easy, medium, hard, and very hard RDKs were held constant across trials.
For the remaining 50 participants, the locations of the tasks varied from trial to trial in a Random fashion.
Power analysis for a chi-square test of uniformity, used for analyzing the selection orders, indicated that an N of 47 provides 95% power for detecting a difference from random responding.
We aimed to collect at least 45 participants in each condition or as many as the testing period would allow.
The experiment was programmed in HTML and Javascript using the jsPsych package (De Leeuw, 2015) and administered over the participant's browser.
Human Research Participant was approved by the University of Melbourne Human Research Ethics Committee (ID 2056156.3).
Data for Experiment 1 were collected in 2020.
Procedure & Design.
text.formatted: Procedure & Design.

text.text: In each condition, participants completed multiple trials in which they were asked to select and complete as many RDKs as possible.
On each trial, participants were shown a set of four labeled RDKs (see Figure 1).
text.formatted: On each trial, participants were shown a set of four labeled RDKs (see Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">1</ref>).

text.text: The labels corresponded to the coherence of the RDK; that is, the proportion of dots moving in a coherent direction was set to 80%, 50%, 20%, and 0% for the Easy, Medium, Hard, and Very Hard tasks, respectively.
2 A coherence of 80% means that 80% of the of dots moved in the same direction (either left or right) over the life of the RDK.

Once the correct direction of motion was selected by the participant the experiment returned to the selection screen with the previously completed tasks greyed out and unavailable for selection.
Participants first completed 10 trials with a long deadline (30 sec) to help participants learn the task and explore strategies.
Participants then completed 30 trials with a 6 second deadline.
The short deadline was set based on pilot testing to allow for three tasks to be completed on average.

Participants completed the experiment by clicking a link with a uniquely generated ID code; the link could have been used multiple times, and participants were able to exit the experiment at any time.
Consequently, the data file contained partially completed data for some subjects that needed to be identified and removed.
We additionally screened the data for participants who had less than chance accuracy on the easiest RDK indicating computer problems or a misunderstanding of task directions.
We removed these participants (N = 3) from further analysis leaving 47 and 50 in the Fixed and Random Location conditions, respectively.
We conducted a number of manipulation checks to ensure that deadline and task difficulty were manipulated effectively.

We first checked that the deadline resulted in a fewer number of task completions (i.e., if deadline does not reduce task completions, 3 We have also replicated the present results without the penalty for an incorrect RDK response.

Removing the error penalty had no qualitative effect on the results but does run the risk that participants approach the more difficult judgments with a series of fast guesses.
Penalizing error responses reduces the likelihood of this strategy, even though our empirical results showed no evidence that participants employed it.

We then examined the accuracy and total time taken to make an accurate RDK decision for the Easy, Medium, Hard, and Very Hard tasks demonstrating that accuracy and RT were ordered in line with our manipulation of coherence.
After establishing the effectiveness of the experimental manipulations, we examined the optimality of the selected order in several ways.
We first computed the marginal distribution of each of the tasks (i.e., the proportion of times each task was selected in each order).
We checked that the resulting marginal response probabilities differed from random responding.
We then examined how far the selection orders were from the optimal SPT scheduling policy by calculating the swap distance between the observed schedule and an easiest-to-hardest order.
We additionally analyzed whether the first selected option was the easiest option of the set and whether the entire order followed an SPT policy.
We report how we determined our sample size, all data exclusions, all manipulations, and all measures in the study.

text.text: Experiment 1 was preregistered.
The design and analysis plan for Experiment 1 is available at 10.17605/OSF.IO/PCJSB; hypotheses were exploratory.
We depart from the preregistered plan in several respects.
First, we initially specified Bayesian parameter estimation with a hierarchical model and DIC-based model comparison.
We instead report frequentist mixed-effects models and ANOVAs.
The comparisons tested are the ones specified in the preregistration; the change concerns only the inferential framework.
Second, we preregistered coherence levels of .8, .5, .1 and 0; the experiments were run with levels of .8, .5, .2 and 0.
Third, we specified excluding participants who did not complete all trials.
We additionally excluded participants who performed at or below chance on the easiest random dot kinematogram; exclusions are reported in full in the Method.

text.text: For each participant, we computed the average rank order across trials for selecting the tasks.

For example, if a particular task (e.g., the easy task) was selected first on all trials, its average rank order would be 1, whereas if it had been selected at random, such that it would have been equally likely to be attempted first, second, third, or fourth, with a likelihood 1/4 each, its average rank order would be (1+2+3+4)/4 = 2.5.
From these average orders, we computed the marginal probabilities for each task selected in each order for each participant (see Figure 3).

Completely optimal performance would be indicated by a value of 1 on the main diagonal and 0 on the off diagonal.

When tasks are explicitly labeled according to their difficulty, participants select and complete those tasks in a near-optimal fashion consistent with a shortest-to-longest processing order.
This occurs to an even greater extent when there is a deadline that prevents completion of all of the tasks in line with an increase in motivation.
Further, when the tasks are randomized from trial to trial, adding an additional search cost, there is a decrease in the optimality of the scheduled order.

This latter result suggests that any effect which increases the amount of time needed to determine the difficulty of a task should decrease the extent to which the scheduled order matches or approaches an SPT order.

Although there are tasks in which the duration of a task may be known (even approximately), there are also many scenarios in which the duration or difficulty of a task is not known a priori and must be estimated at a glance.
For example, the proximity of pairs of aircraft in a display provides a cue to an air traffic controller about what conflict to address first.

Selecting from a series of research articles to read or assignments to mark may involve a quick assessment of length or writing style or evaluating which insurance to buy may involve a quick appraisal of the readability of a company's website.
Experiment 2 examined whether participants select tasks in an optimal fashion when no explicit labeling of difficulty was provided.
In Experiment 1, each RDK was presented on the selection screen along with a label indicating its difficulty.
In Experiment 2, each RDK was presented on the selection screen without a label, moving according to its coherence in a randomly selected left-right direction.
Once selected, the other (non-selected) RDKs stopped moving and the selected RDK direction was randomly resampled.
Participants had to respond to the selected task as in Experiment 1.
In order to apply an ordered prioritization policy, an observer would need to spend part of the time budget extracting information about task difficulty (up to some precision).
This time trades off against remaining time needed to make the selection and to complete each task.
To foreshadow the results, making the tasks dynamic and unlabeled moved selection away from an SPT first order, such that selection deviated from SPT and was closer to random responding.

text.text: We tested 105 participants recruited through the Melbourne School of Psychological Sciences Research Experience Pool (Mean age = 19.17, age range = 17-33, 81 F, 24 M).
Participants were reimbursed with credit toward completion of a first year psychology subject.

Five subjects were excluded from the Fixed condition and eight were removed from the Random condition for having less than chance accuracy on the easiest RDK leaving 46 participants in each condition.
The experiment was programmed in HTML and Javascript using the jsPsych package (De Leeuw, 2015) and administered over the participant's browser.
Data for Experiment 2 were collected in 2021 under the same ethics approval as Experiment 1.

text.text: The design, procedure, and data analysis steps of Experiment 2 were identical to Experiment 1, with the exception that instead of labeling the RDK difficulty, RDKs were presented as moving dynamic displays on the selection screen.
Consequently, the difficulty of each task had to be inferred by integrating the motion of the random dots.
Once selected, the unselected RDKs stopped moving and the direction was resampled for the selected RDK.

text.text: Under a deadline, there was some organisation along the diagonal; in both the fixed and random location conditions, the hard and very hard conditions tended to be scheduled third and fourth.
This accords with the SPT policy, but the two easiest tasks were not consistently scheduled first.
One explanation is that participants are unable to tell apart the RDKs at the levels of coherence that we used.
In Appendix B, we report the results of an experiment where we asked people to select the same dynamic RDKs from easiest to hardest, without requiring any task completion after selection.

Removing task completion left ample time to select all four tasks within the 6 second deadline, and the results indicated that participants were able to successfully order the RDKs when asked to do so.
In light of those results, the explanation is that participants are unable to tell apart the RDKs when there is limited time to do so.
It is plausible that the added time pressure of completing each task reduced the precision of the observations, leading to more random selection from among the three easiest tasks.
Presumably, among all of the decisions, the most difficult task is easy to quickly identify and drop.

text.text: The slow time course of encoding suggests that a representation of task difficulty can only be established with lower precision in a short time window.
Hence, one explanation of the present results is that the additional sampling time needed to develop a precise representation of RDK difficulty was not offset by the benefit of an SPT order.
That is, the difference in number of tasks completed between an SPT and random order was not large enough to offset the cost of sampling.
Because developing a precise representation of difficulty takes time, which is paid from the overall time budget, it may in fact be more optimal to stop observing and to select any task (cf.
Drugowitsch, Moreno-Bote, Churchland, Shadlen, & Pouget, 2012) than it is to attempt to order the tasks and apply an SPT strategy.

text.text: We sought to further characterize this finding by removing observation time from the time budget.
This should promote the development of a more precise representation of difficulty (up to the precision limit) consequently promoting a switch from more random to more SPT scheduling.
To test this prediction, in Experiment 3, we limited the observation time to a fixed time window and then swept out the window to allow more observation time in some blocks than in others.
We then compare how scheduling changes with increased free observation time.
In Experiment 3, observers were shown a dynamic display that was presented for a variable observation time window.
This time was not counted against the deadline for the trial.
We used two sets of observation windows, presented as a blocked within-subjects manipulation, randomized across subjects.
In the first set, the observation windows were 200 ms, 400 ms, or 800 ms.
The shortest and longest windows bracketed the average integration time window ( 400 ms) (P. L. Smith & Lilburn, 2020); hence, we refer to this condition as the Bracketed (200|400|800) condition.
text.formatted: The shortest and longest windows bracketed the average integration time window ( 400 ms) (P. L. Smith & Lilburn, 2020); hence, we refer to this condition as the Bracketed (200|400|800) condition.

text.text: For the second set, the observation windows were 400 ms, 800 ms, and 1600 ms.
These timings are roughly anchored to the 10%, 30% and 50% selection RT quantiles observed in our selection only experiment (see Appendix B).
Hereafter, we refer to this second condition as the Anchored (400|800|1600) condition.
As shown in the appendix, these quantiles were 567 ms, 931 ms, and 1460 ms in actuality; however, the duplication of windows between-subjects allows for a built-in replication of those conditions.

Sampling in log spacing across two sets of observation windows also allows for investigation across a large range of observation times and is further theoretically motivated as noise accumulates as the square root of time in diffusive evidence accumulation (P. L. Smith & Ratcliff, 2025); hence, the increments of precision growth are equally spaced.

After the integration window, all of the displays stopped moving until a selection was made; thus difficulty can only be judged during the integration window.
Selection can be made at any time, either during the integration window or after the RDKs have stopped moving.
After selection, that RDK direction was resampled and the participant had to respond with the RDK direction (until correct as in Experiments 1 and 2), before being returned to the selection screen.
We made two other changes to ensure that participants were incentivized to sample the RDK during selection.
First, the deadline was decreased from 6 seconds to 3 seconds, and second, the penalty for an incorrect RDK response was increased to from .5 s to 2 s.
Both of these manipulations work to offset the cost of sampling by increasing the amount by which an SPT strategy allows a greater number of task completions over a random strategy.
That is, should a difficult task be selected first, the penalty for guessing incorrectly would take out over half of the remaining time.
We expect the distance from an SPT optimal strategy should decrease as the observation window increases allowing for a better representation of task difficulty.

text.text: For each observation window, participants completed 3 practice trials, which are not analyzed, 10 Long Deadline trials with a 30 second deadline, and 30 short deadline trials with a 3 second deadline.
On each trial, the set of RDKs were presented in motion on the selection screen for the duration of the observation window (or until selection).
After the observation window, the RDKs stopped moving and remained static until selection.
The direction of the selected RDK was then resampled, and the participant had to respond with the direction of the selected RDK.
If an incorrect response was made, the task paused for 2.5 seconds, the direction was resampled, and the participant had to respond to the same RDK again.
This was repeated until a correct response was made or until the deadline was reached for the trial.
After a correct response, the participant returned to the selection screen and selected another RDK for completion.
All remaining task settings were identical to Experiment 2.

text.text: Experiment 3 was not preregistered.
Its design follows directly from Experiments 1 and 2 and was motivated by the results reported here, and all of its analyses should be regarded as exploratory.
All three experiments were conducted online in participants' own web browsers.

The data for Experiments 1 and 2 were collected in 2020 and 2021 respectively, before large language models (LLMs) were generally available, and we regard AI-generated responding as implausible for those datasets.
Experiment 3 was conducted in 2026, when LLM tools were widely available.
The task format offers substantial protection in all three experiments.
Participants were not asked to produce free text or to answer questions whose content could be generated externally.
Each trial required a sequence of mouse clicks on randomly moving dot displays followed by speeded keyboard responses.

The relevant information was present only transiently on screen and only in the stimulus display, so responding on the participant's behalf would require real-time visual access to the display rather than access to text.
Responses are uninformative without that display: the correct direction was resampled on every attempt, so no fixed response pattern would succeed.

Participants were recruited through university research participation schemes rather than open online marketplaces, and were reimbursed with course credit rather than payment, which further reduces the incentive for automated participation.
Additionally, we used a performance-based exclusion rule that would identify non-genuine responding.

In this section, we take steps toward a cognitive process model of scheduling order by drawing on a related model of preference ranking.
The Plackett-Luce model (Luce, 1959; Plackett, 1975) is a statistical model used for analyzing ranking data (i.e., orders of preferences from a set of options).

text.text: Scheduling order can be thought of as ranked preferences, where the order is the preference of completing a particular task in a particular sequence.
In the Plackett-Luce model, each task is associated with an underlying "strength" value, ν.
In Luce's choice rule, the probability of selecting an option, i, is found by normalizing its strength model by the sum of the strengths of all of the options:
The Plackett-Luce model provides a generalization of Luce's (1959) choice rule by providing a probability of selecting a particular ranked sequence.

The strength parameters can be estimated using maximum likelihood estimation (see e.g., P. H. Lee & Yu, 2013) fitting the model to the set of scheduling selections.

To summarize, we envisage a model in which the precision of the observation contributes to the strength parameter, which is then used by the Luce's choice rule to implement the selection policy.
As shown in Experiment 3, the precision of the representation determines the optimality of scheduling.
One might alternatively posit that the representation could be fixed with stochasticity only entering in through Luce's choice rule.
Or alternatively that a deterministic decision rule could be combined with noisy inputs.
