In this paper, we have introduced a novel paradigm for studying human scheduling behavior in which cognitive work is required to progress toward the completion of tasks.
All tasks were presented simultaneously but could only be completed one at a time.
We recorded both performance (accuracy and task completion time) and scheduling behaviour (the order in which they are completed or attempted).
The advantage of this new paradigm is that it allows for assessment of scheduling prioritization choices independent of the completion of each task.
Consequently, the difficulty, value, and type of task can be manipulated independently alongside the overall goal.
This allows for a comparison to optimal benchmarks developed through the application of Scheduling Theory or dynamic allocation indices, such as the Gittins index.
A further benefit is that under some task settings, the task shares processes with classic cognitive tasks that also evoke serial processing such as visual search and perceptual categorization.
Our paradigm is also broadly reminiscent of "real-world" tasks requiring the completion of several subgoals.
We demonstrated that the quality of the observation difficulty trades off against the implementation of an optimal schedule.
We additionally introduce a model of scheduling choices that links scheduling with models of preference ranking.
The primary value of this analysis is in the conceptualization of prioritization and scheduling as a choice behavior.
This allows the unique identification of each task with a strength parameter, ν.
The value of ν can be thought to capture how well each task contributes to the achievement of the scheduling goal (e.g., completing as many tasks as possible).
Ultimately, we would hope to elaborate the factors that contribute to the evaluation of task strength.

Three approaches that can inform this endeavour are Wickens' modeling of dynamic visual attention in graphical displays (i.e., SEEV model, Wickens, 2015), multitask management in the STOM model (Wickens et al., 2015), and Ballard and colleagues work on multiple goal pursuit (Ballard, Farrell, & Neal, 2018a; Ballard et al., 2022; Ballard, Vancouver, & Neal, 2018; Ballard, Yeo, Loft, et al., 2016).
text.formatted: Three approaches that can inform this endeavour are Wickens' modeling of dynamic visual attention in graphical displays (i.e., SEEV model, <ref type="bibr" target="#b134">Wickens, 2015)</ref>, multitask management in the STOM model <ref type="bibr" target="#b136">(Wickens et al., 2015)</ref>, and Ballard and colleagues work on multiple goal pursuit <ref type="bibr">(Ballard, Farrell, & Neal, 2018a;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Ballard et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Ballard, Vancouver, & Neal, 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">Ballard, Yeo, Loft, et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: We address these extensions below.
What determines the value of the strength parameter?
Many models assume that information is processed serially but do not make a strong commitment to the order in which information is processed.

For example, in some designs (e.g., whole report), serial comparison is assumed to occur in a reading order dictated by the spatial location of the targets (Schneider & Shiffrin, 1977); here the order of processing follows a frequently executed order.
text.formatted: For example, in some designs (e.g., whole report), serial comparison is assumed to occur in a reading order dictated by the spatial location of the targets <ref type="bibr" target="#b107">(Schneider & Shiffrin, 1977)</ref>; here the order of processing follows a frequently executed order.

text.text: In Tversky's (1972) Elimination-by-Aspect theory, choice alternatives are compared on the basis of individual dimensions, and options without specific desired features are dropped.
text.formatted: In <ref type="bibr" target="#b129">Tversky's (1972)</ref> Elimination-by-Aspect theory, choice alternatives are compared on the basis of individual dimensions, and options without specific desired features are dropped.

text.text: For instance, in deciding which guitar to purchase, one might first start by eliminating all guitars without an offset body (e.g., stratocasters or Les Paul's), and then proceeding to compare the remaining options (e.g., Jazzmaster, Firebird) on the presence of a floating bridge.
Hence, elimination-by-aspects proceeds sequentially but does not specify an order in which attributes are compared.
Humans and other organisms often have some awareness of how important different cues are for decisions (either through learning or evolution; Sloman & Sloman, 2009).
text.formatted: Humans and other organisms often have some awareness of how important different cues are for decisions (either through learning or evolution; <ref type="bibr" target="#b114">Sloman & Sloman, 2009)</ref>.

text.text: Heuristic models of decision making, such as Take-the-Best (Gigerenzer, Hoffrage, & Kleinbolting, 1991), typically specify that cues or information sources are searched in order of validity, stopping at the first cue that differentiates the options (Payne, Bettman, & Johnson, 1993).
text.formatted: Heuristic models of decision making, such as Take-the-Best <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Gigerenzer, Hoffrage, & Kleinbolting, 1991)</ref>, typically specify that cues or information sources are searched in order of validity, stopping at the first cue that differentiates the options <ref type="bibr" target="#b87">(Payne, Bettman, & Johnson, 1993)</ref>.

text.text: Take-the-best is an example of a lexicographic strategy, or heuristic (e.g., alphabetical or numerical order, Fishburn, 1974; Gigerenzer et al., 1991; Lafond, Lacouture, & Cohen, 2009; Luan, Schooler, & Gigerenzer, 2011; Payne et al., 1993; Trabasso, Rollins, & Shaughnessy, 1971).
text.formatted: Take-the-best is an example of a lexicographic strategy, or heuristic (e.g., alphabetical or numerical order, <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Fishburn, 1974;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Gigerenzer et al., 1991;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">Lafond, Lacouture, & Cohen, 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b70">Luan, Schooler, & Gigerenzer, 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b87">Payne et al., 1993;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b128">Trabasso, Rollins, & Shaughnessy, 1971)</ref>.

text.text: Decision trees (Trabasso et al., 1971), such as those used in medical triage (Cook, 2001), are another class of models in which decision accuracy is maximized by ordering cues from most to least diagnostic. Luan et al. (2011) defined a class of fast-and-frugal trees that assist decision makers by segmenting processing into a series of sequential decisions, allowing for termination of the decision-making process after each step. Luan et al. (2011) showed that a tree with steps ordered by diagnosticity produced a higher final decision sensitivity than trees using a different order.
text.formatted: Decision trees <ref type="bibr" target="#b128">(Trabasso et al., 1971)</ref>, such as those used in medical triage <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Cook, 2001)</ref>, are another class of models in which decision accuracy is maximized by ordering cues from most to least diagnostic. <ref type="bibr" target="#b70">Luan et al. (2011)</ref> defined a class of fast-and-frugal trees that assist decision makers by segmenting processing into a series of sequential decisions, allowing for termination of the decision-making process after each step. <ref type="bibr" target="#b70">Luan et al. (2011)</ref> showed that a tree with steps ordered by diagnosticity produced a higher final decision sensitivity than trees using a different order.

text.text: Hence, ordering the steps by diagnosticity provides one measure, based on decision accuracy, that can form the basis of rational responding.
Some visual attention models also invoke cue relevance as a basis for determining processing order.

For instance, in Shiffrin and Geisler's (1973) model of visual target detection, serial search is assumed to begin with locations that indicate the most-probable presence of a target and then proceed in order of decreasing likelihood of target presence until a target is identified.
text.formatted: For instance, in <ref type="bibr" target="#b112">Shiffrin and Geisler's (1973)</ref> model of visual target detection, serial search is assumed to begin with locations that indicate the most-probable presence of a target and then proceed in order of decreasing likelihood of target presence until a target is identified.

text.text: A relevant question is then what determines cue relevance.

Multiple goal pursuit offers another perspective on how agents allocate resources between different competing tasks (e.g., Ballard, Farrell, & Neal, 2018a; Ballard et al., 2022; Ballard, Vancouver, & Neal, 2018; Ballard, Yeo, Loft, et al., 2016; Ballard, Yeo, Neal, & Farrell, 2016; Hotaling, 2020; Neal et al., 2017; Schmidt & DeShon, 2007; Vancouver et al., 2010).
text.formatted: Multiple goal pursuit offers another perspective on how agents allocate resources between different competing tasks (e.g., <ref type="bibr">Ballard, Farrell, & Neal, 2018a;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Ballard et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Ballard, Vancouver, & Neal, 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">Ballard, Yeo, Loft, et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Ballard, Yeo, Neal, & Farrell, 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">Hotaling, 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b83">Neal et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b106">Schmidt & DeShon, 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b130">Vancouver et al., 2010)</ref>.

text.text: In a typical multiple goal pursuit task, participants allocate a limited resource to one of usually two options.
That option then progresses toward some goal state.
Options can differ in how rapidly they approach the goal state (e.g., rate of progress), how far away the goal state is (e.g., deadline), and the value of each goal.
Multiple goal pursuit tasks also vary approach or avoidance goals, which affect how people tend to allocate resources (Ballard, Farrell, & Neal, 2018b).
text.formatted: Multiple goal pursuit tasks also vary approach or avoidance goals, which affect how people tend to allocate resources <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Ballard, Farrell, & Neal, 2018b)</ref>.

text.text: One critical difference between the multiple goal pursuit paradigm and the present paradigm is the time scale of the tasks.
Our task sits closer to the time scale of attention allocation tasks where selection (attending) and completion (processing) of tasks occurs over a few seconds.
Multiple goal pursuit tasks, on the other hand, typically progress over a longer time scale (e.g., an hour long experimental session).

Similar to the attentional literature, "effort" in multiple goal pursuit denotes the subjective expected demand of completing a task, which can depend on anticipated physical exertion, mental workload and opportunity costs.
"Value" or intrinsic reward, modulated by temporal discounting, is also a central factor determining how people allocate resources.
A key result is that under a deadline, people preferentially allocate resources to tasks that they expect they can complete.

A typical finding is that participants will allocate resources to tasks which are further from completion until it is clear that such as task cannot be completed before the deadline; from that point, the other task is preferred (Ballard, Farrell, & Neal, 2018a).
text.formatted: A typical finding is that participants will allocate resources to tasks which are further from completion until it is clear that such as task cannot be completed before the deadline; from that point, the other task is preferred <ref type="bibr">(Ballard, Farrell, & Neal, 2018a)</ref>.

text.text: Under longer deadlines, people tend to balance resources more evenly across tasks (Ballard, Farrell, & Neal, 2018a).
text.formatted: Under longer deadlines, people tend to balance resources more evenly across tasks <ref type="bibr">(Ballard, Farrell, & Neal, 2018a)</ref>.

text.text: These results suggest that strength could be modeled as a function that diminishes with effort and increases as deadlines loom, again balancing expectation and reward.

In our paradigm, Fixed Location mappings increase expectancy and reduce the attentional effort required to access difficulty information-consistent with findings that visual attention is directed more efficiently to high-probability locations resulting from learned spatial regularities (Xu, Los, & Theeuwes, 2021).
text.formatted: In our paradigm, Fixed Location mappings increase expectancy and reduce the attentional effort required to access difficulty information-consistent with findings that visual attention is directed more efficiently to high-probability locations resulting from learned spatial regularities <ref type="bibr" target="#b144">(Xu, Los, & Theeuwes, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: In contrast, random location arrangements lower expectancy and increase search costs by forcing broader scanning and reallocation of gaze.

Similarly, difficulty labels enhance the salience of the task's difficulty attribute and lower the variability associated with the representation of difficulty, facilitating rapid top-down search and accurate extraction of difficulty information, in line with evidence that categorical labels improve memory precision and guide attention (Xu et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Similarly, difficulty labels enhance the salience of the task's difficulty attribute and lower the variability associated with the representation of difficulty, facilitating rapid top-down search and accurate extraction of difficulty information, in line with evidence that categorical labels improve memory precision and guide attention <ref type="bibr" target="#b144">(Xu et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: By contrast, when difficulty is conveyed through motion coherence in dynamic RDK patches, the same information must be inferred from low-level perceptual features, which are noisier, less directly connected to the representation of decision-relevant information, and take time to develop.

These manipulations impose different demands on attribute acquisition, the perceptual and attentional effort to locate and extract the relevant cue (Bundesen, 1990; Palmer, Verghese, & Pavel, 2000), and the learning and representational effort to associate a cue with its underlying attribute (Dayan & Kakade, 2000; Niv, Daw, Joel, & Dayan, 2007).
text.formatted: These manipulations impose different demands on attribute acquisition, the perceptual and attentional effort to locate and extract the relevant cue <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Bundesen, 1990;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b86">Palmer, Verghese, & Pavel, 2000)</ref>, and the learning and representational effort to associate a cue with its underlying attribute <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Dayan & Kakade, 2000;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b84">Niv, Daw, Joel, & Dayan, 2007)</ref>.

text.text: When access latency is high (random locations) and mapping cost is high (motion cues), acquisition is slow and error-prone; when both are low (fixed + label), attribute acquisition is rapid and reliable.

In light of these results, the integrated strength parameter in the Plackett-Luce model should reflect the combined output of multiple valuation systems (Rangel, Camerer, & Montague, 2008) rather than reflecting a direct readout of utility (e.g., from classical decision theory, Bernoulli, 1954; von Neumann & Morgenstern, 1944).
text.formatted: In light of these results, the integrated strength parameter in the Plackett-Luce model should reflect the combined output of multiple valuation systems <ref type="bibr" target="#b96">(Rangel, Camerer, & Montague, 2008)</ref> rather than reflecting a direct readout of utility (e.g., from classical decision theory, <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Bernoulli, 1954;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b132">von Neumann & Morgenstern, 1944)</ref>.

text.text: These systems act on attributes acquired during the attentional stage, and could include goal-directed processes that compute utilities from an internal model of the environment (Daw, Niv, & Dayan, 2005), learned response biases from learned cue-outcome associations (Dayan, Niv, Seymour, & Daw, 2006), and habitual tendencies based on cached action values (Balleine & O'Doherty, 2010; Dolan & Dayan, 2013).
text.formatted: These systems act on attributes acquired during the attentional stage, and could include goal-directed processes that compute utilities from an internal model of the environment <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Daw, Niv, & Dayan, 2005)</ref>, learned response biases from learned cue-outcome associations <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Dayan, Niv, Seymour, & Daw, 2006)</ref>, and habitual tendencies based on cached action values <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Balleine & O'Doherty, 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Dolan & Dayan, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Arbitration between these systems depends on the reliability of available information and the computational cost of deliberation (Kool, Cushman, & Gershman, 2018).
text.formatted: Arbitration between these systems depends on the reliability of available information and the computational cost of deliberation <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">(Kool, Cushman, & Gershman, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Consequently, high ν values would indicate tasks that are perceptually easy to access, align with immediate goals, and impose low effort costs; low ν values emerge when acquisition is costly, urgency is low, effort is high, or uncertainty discounts discriminability between tasks.
Observation of task variables is made through the allocation of a limited capacity selective attention mechanism that collects evidence over time.
The selection and encoding of stimulus attributes is shaped by the interaction of bottom-up salience, top-down goals, and history-based influences.

Wickens' SEEV (Salience, Effort, Expectancy, Value) model (Wickens & McCarley, 2008) outlines four factors that drive the allocation of visual attention across dynamic displays (e.g., while driving, writing code, or flying a plane).
text.formatted: Wickens' SEEV (Salience, Effort, Expectancy, Value) model <ref type="bibr" target="#b138">(Wickens & McCarley, 2008)</ref> outlines four factors that drive the allocation of visual attention across dynamic displays (e.g., while driving, writing code, or flying a plane).

text.text: Observers in these tasks must decide what aspects of the display to focus on and when.
The "attractiveness" or strength of each location in the display is a weighted combination of perceptual salience, effort, expectancy and value (Wickens & McCarley, 2008).
text.formatted: The "attractiveness" or strength of each location in the display is a weighted combination of perceptual salience, effort, expectancy and value <ref type="bibr" target="#b138">(Wickens & McCarley, 2008)</ref>.

text.text: Salience refers to the intrinsic attention-grabbing natures of a task cues.
More salient cues attract attention, all else being equal, which naturally draws attention away from more valid cues (Itti & Koch, 2000; Kruschke & Johansen, 1999; Little & Lewandowsky, 2012).
text.formatted: More salient cues attract attention, all else being equal, which naturally draws attention away from more valid cues <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">(Itti & Koch, 2000;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">Kruschke & Johansen, 1999;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">Little & Lewandowsky, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: When examined across time, the initial attention-grab of salient cues may require a shift away to more valid cues (Lamberts, 1995 (Lamberts, , 1998 (Lamberts, , 2000)); hence, attention is dynamically allocated moment to moment and with learning, shifts toward more-goal relevant cues and locations.
text.formatted: When examined across time, the initial attention-grab of salient cues may require a shift away to more valid cues <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">(Lamberts, 1995</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">(Lamberts, , 1998</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">(Lamberts, , 2000))</ref>; hence, attention is dynamically allocated moment to moment and with learning, shifts toward more-goal relevant cues and locations.

text.text: Expectancy reflects the belief that attending to a particular task will provide valuable information and can also reflect the rate at which information changes in a display (consequently, requiring greater attention Carbonell, Ward, & Senders, 2007).
text.formatted: Expectancy reflects the belief that attending to a particular task will provide valuable information and can also reflect the rate at which information changes in a display (consequently, requiring greater attention <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Carbonell, Ward, & Senders, 2007)</ref>.

text.text: Value captures the importance of that information given the objective of sampling or the cost of missing information at that location (Wickens, Helton, Hollands, & Banbury, 2021).
text.formatted: Value captures the importance of that information given the objective of sampling or the cost of missing information at that location <ref type="bibr" target="#b137">(Wickens, Helton, Hollands, & Banbury, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Finally, effort denotes the physical cost of shifting gaze (i.e., physical effort) or mental focus (i.e., mental effort) to the task.

Ideal dwell time/fixation duration and scan path, can be determined by considering the weighted product of expectancy and value (e.g., expected value Wickens, 2015), but actual attention allocation in a display requires considering all four factors.
text.formatted: Ideal dwell time/fixation duration and scan path, can be determined by considering the weighted product of expectancy and value (e.g., expected value <ref type="bibr" target="#b134">Wickens, 2015)</ref>, but actual attention allocation in a display requires considering all four factors.

text.text: For more complex tasks, that require decisions beyond where to look at the present moment, Wickens et al. (2015) developed the Strategic Task Overload Management (STOM) model.
text.formatted: For more complex tasks, that require decisions beyond where to look at the present moment, <ref type="bibr" target="#b136">Wickens et al. (2015)</ref> developed the Strategic Task Overload Management (STOM) model.

text.text: STOM combines various task attributes (including the salience of task arrival/availability, task interest -similar to the value variable in SEEV, task priority, and task difficulty or demand) to calculate whether an operator will continue to focus on the present task or switch to a new task.
Thus, in the same manner that SEEV predicts attentional engagement with or switching between visual objects in a display, STOM predicts staying or switching between different tasks.

SEEV and STOM have been successful in predicting a variety of visual and cognitive tunneling behaviors, respectively; that is, a tendency to stick with current fixation or current tasks rather than switch to other important visual displays or tasks (Adler & Benbunan-Fich, 2012; Horrey & Wickens, 2007; Raby & Wickens, 1994; Wickens & Alexander, 2009; Wickens et al., 2021).
text.formatted: SEEV and STOM have been successful in predicting a variety of visual and cognitive tunneling behaviors, respectively; that is, a tendency to stick with current fixation or current tasks rather than switch to other important visual displays or tasks <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Adler & Benbunan-Fich, 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">Horrey & Wickens, 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b95">Raby & Wickens, 1994;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b135">Wickens & Alexander, 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b137">Wickens et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: There are differences between allocating selective attention, which can be achieved on the order of milliseconds, and managing multiple tasks, each of which can take seconds or minutes (or longer) to complete.
Visual areas of interest can also be processed in parallel in many situations (e.g., visual search, Wolfe et al., 1990).
text.formatted: Visual areas of interest can also be processed in parallel in many situations (e.g., visual search, <ref type="bibr" target="#b143">Wolfe et al., 1990)</ref>.

text.text: However, in other contexts, visual attention is forced to proceed serially by factors such as spatial separation or the inclusion of distracting elements (e.g., Logan, 1996; Moneer & Little, 2026).
text.formatted: However, in other contexts, visual attention is forced to proceed serially by factors such as spatial separation or the inclusion of distracting elements (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b69">Logan, 1996;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b79">Moneer & Little, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: For example, dimensional processing in categorization has been demonstrated to proceed serially across a number of different stimulus types (Cheng, McCarthy, Wang, Palmeri, & Little, 2018; Fifić, Little, & Nosofsky, 2010; Griffiths, Blunden, & Little, 2017; Little, Eidels, Fific, & Wang, 2018; Little & Lewandowsky, 2012; Little, Nosofsky, & Denton, 2011; Little, Nosofsky, Donkin, & Denton, 2013; Moneer, Wang, & Little, 2016).
text.formatted: For example, dimensional processing in categorization has been demonstrated to proceed serially across a number of different stimulus types <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Cheng, McCarthy, Wang, Palmeri, & Little, 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">Fifić, Little, & Nosofsky, 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">Griffiths, Blunden, & Little, 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">Little, Eidels, Fific, & Wang, 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">Little & Lewandowsky, 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">Little, Nosofsky, & Denton, 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b67">Little, Nosofsky, Donkin, & Denton, 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b80">Moneer, Wang, & Little, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: In some experiments, there tends to be a bias to first process one of the dimensions over the other (see e.g., Little et al., 2011), which naturally leads to a question of how dimensions are prioritized for processing.
text.formatted: In some experiments, there tends to be a bias to first process one of the dimensions over the other (see e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">Little et al., 2011)</ref>, which naturally leads to a question of how dimensions are prioritized for processing.

text.text: Managing a set of tasks or allocating spatial selective attention both require an implicit or explicit decision about where to allocate resources next.
From a scheduling theory perspective, optimally ordering tasks requires additionally considering the goal, which would determine factors such as expectancy (in SEEV) or task priority (in STOM).
We frame scheduling as a decision task and adapt a model of ranking preference choice to capture variability in the observed completion orders.
This places scheduling alongside other multi-alternative decision tasks that have recently received increased interest.
A key point of difference is that scheduling prioritization orders involve several sequential choices with a choice set that decreases in cardinality with each decision.
The Plackett-Luce model offers a natural approach for modeling this type of decision, but we foresee a benefit in treating the decision process as a sequential sampling problem.

This would allow the application of successful models of choice response time, such as racing diffusion models (Brown & Heathcote, 2008; P. L. Smith, in press; Tillman, Van Zandt, & Logan, 2020) that would allow us to predict scheduling decisions (order) as well as the RT distributions associated with those decisions (Hawkins, Forstmann, Wagenmakers, Ratcliff, & Brown, 2015; Ratcliff, Smith, Brown, & McKoon, 2016).
text.formatted: This would allow the application of successful models of choice response time, such as racing diffusion models <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Brown & Heathcote, 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr">P. L. Smith, in press;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b123">Tillman, Van Zandt, & Logan, 2020)</ref> that would allow us to predict scheduling decisions (order) as well as the RT distributions associated with those decisions <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">(Hawkins, Forstmann, Wagenmakers, Ratcliff, & Brown, 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b99">Ratcliff, Smith, Brown, & McKoon, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: In scheduling decision making, the drift rate could be interpreted as the moment-to-moment evidence for prioritizing a to-be-scheduled task (Cisek, 2007; P. L. Smith & Ratcliff, 2004), while boundary settings reflect speed-accuracy trade-offs.
text.formatted: In scheduling decision making, the drift rate could be interpreted as the moment-to-moment evidence for prioritizing a to-be-scheduled task <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Cisek, 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b118">P. L. Smith & Ratcliff, 2004)</ref>, while boundary settings reflect speed-accuracy trade-offs.

text.text: Since each scheduling decision affects the time remaining for future decisions and task completion, a suboptimal scheduling choice can lead to increased downstream time pressure.
Decoupling the effects of drift rate and boundary would provide some insight into how time pressure affects scheduling decisions.
Our participants were young, predominantly female undergraduate students.
We have no reason to expect that our most important result, that a longer observation window improves scheduling, to be specific to this group as the mechanism we propose is a general one.
Namely, prioritization decisions are limited by how precisely task difficulty can be represented.

We would expect the same pattern in any population able to perform the motion discrimination task, but factors such as motion sensitivity, affecting the ability to integrate moving random dots, and neurodivergence, affect motivation, might increase noise and lead to correspondingly worse schedules.
Testing was conducted online in participants' own browsers, so screen size, viewing distance, refresh rate, and ambient lighting varied across participants and were not under our control.
This variation adds noise to the results but is most likely to have affected Experiments 1 and 2 since Experiment 3 was manipulated observation windows within participants.
The same argument applies to other factors such as motivation, task engagement, and sensitivity to incentives.
Participants almost certainly did not experience the deadline as equally pressing.

The same six-second limit will bind tightly on someone whose motion discrimination is slow or error-prone and leave room to spare for someone faster, and participants will also have differed in how much urgency they felt and how hard they pushed.
This heterogeneity is expected.
And again, less of an issue in Experiment 3, where the observation window was manipulated within participants.

Between-participant variation of this kind in Experiment 1 and 2 enters the analysis as sampling variability making the confidence interval on the effect wider, but it cannot produce the pattern of results observed across our experiments because it is not systematically related.

We would expect the effects to replicate in a sample where the deadline bound more or less tightly overall so long that it did effectively bind performance as the number of tasks completed, and hence the absolute room for ordering to matter, would differ (see below).
Our stimuli were RDKs varying in difficulty calibrated so that difficulty was ordered.
We expect the result to generalise to other continuous perceptual signals (e.g., noisy letters masked by dynamic noise) provided the signal accumulates over time in the same way.
Other types of stimuli may not meet the manipulation requirements of our experiment, and we hence make no claims as to their efficacy.

Several features of the procedure can be varied without, we believe, affecting the result: the particular observation windows used (we obtained consistent estimates across two ranges spanning 200 to 1600 ms in independent samples), the number of trials per block, the order of blocks, the response keys, and the particular coherence values, so long as the range remains wide enough that the differences in difficulty are detectable.
By contrast, two features are more important and should be carefully considered.
First, the deadline must be short enough that the order of completion changes how many tasks are finished.
If the deadline is too long, then any order is equivalent to any other order (including random responding).
Second, the error penalty must be large enough that harder tasks are more time-consuming and not merely more error-prone.
Failure to properly penalize an error could result in a shift in strategy to fast guessing.
Finally, our tasks were presented simultaneously, in peripheral vision, where the eyes can only fixate a single patch at a time.
Varying the observation window may change the number of patches that can be inspected rather than the evidence accumulated about any one of them.
Whether the same relationship holds when tasks are presented one at a time, or when the display can be taken in at a single glance, is an open question.
Nevertheless, we have no reason to believe the results depend on any other characteristic of the participants, materials, or context.
Many complex tasks are comprised of multiple sub-tasks that each must be completed for successful goal attainment.
If resources are limited, or if subtasks are contingent on one another, those subtasks cannot be completed at the same time and must be completed sequentially.
Under those constraints, how do people decide what is the appropriate order of task completion?
Assembling a car requires multiple steps, each of which must be performed to perfection.
Assembly order is predetermined and externally imposed; the chassis, body, doors and wheels, must all be manufactured before they can be assembled together.
A key point of this paper is to highlight that behavioral and cognitive tasks are also ordered, and the order may not be externally constrained.
For example, for a student who must submit two reports that are due on the same day, there is no rule dictating the appropriate order of completion.
One student may prefer to write the easy report first, to have something at hand, while another might prefer to start with the harder report to move it out of the way.
Different orders vary in how efficiently they achieve our goals.

text.text: novel paradigm that allows a well-controlled laboratory testing of scheduling decisions.

The new paradigm allows to parametrically manipulate the difficulty of each task, and therefore the time it takes to complete (as well as the number of tasks and many other parameters), and to measure performance, order of completion (scheduling), and any deviance from the optimal schedule.
We demonstrate that the precision of the representation of relevant task factors plays a critical role in the optimality of the resulting prioritization of those tasks.
The paradigm offers rich data that in turn supports model building and deeper theoretical understanding of questions concerning scheduling, and human optimality (or lack thereof).

The Gittins index provides a means to determine the optimal order of selection when there is a single operator (i.e., participant) and when task completion times are stochastic but come from a known distribution (Scully, Grosof, & Harchol-Balter, 2020).
text.formatted: The Gittins index provides a means to determine the optimal order of selection when there is a single operator (i.e., participant) and when task completion times are stochastic but come from a known distribution <ref type="bibr" target="#b108">(Scully, Grosof, & Harchol-Balter, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: In the present experiment, in which the tasks used are non-preemptive, have a common deadline, equivalent rewards, and differ only in completion time, the Gittins index simplifies in a straightforward manner to the Shortest Processing Time First policy, providing a convergent optimal policy.

Note that the Gittins index was developed for tasks in which preemption is available; however, restricting preemption in the present case does not change the optimal order (e.g., even if preemption were allowed, in the present task, the optimal policy would remain SPT).

To illustrate, for tasks in which no work has been started, the general equation for the Gittins index at time, 0, is given as: where ∆ is some unit of time (e.g., the time to the next decision event), V is the value of the task, e -γt is a negative exponential discounting function with rate γ, f (t) is the probability density function of task finishing times, and [1 -F (t)] is the survivor function of the task (i.e., the probability that the task has not finished at time t; Gittins et al., 2011).

text.text: In perceptual decision tasks such as the ones used in this paper, f (t) can be considered the distribution of response times.
The negative exponential function captures the discounting of reward over time.
In our experiments, all tasks have the same value, V = 1, and γ = 0, indicating no discounting of reward over time.
(Monetary rewards are typically shown to be hyperbolically discounted over several months into the future; Green & Myerson, 2004).

When γ → 0 and the hazard function is increasing (indicating an increased likelihood of completing the task as more time is allocated to the task), the Gittins index reduces to Smith's rule, G(t) = V /E(T ), where E(T ) is the expected time to complete the task.
Because h(t) is non-decreasing in t, it implies that E(T ) is non-increasing in t (Townsend, 1990b).

text.text: Because we force participants to repeat the task if the response is incorrect (with an additional time penalty), the total completion time is less skewed compared to a one show decision.
We also apply different levels of difficulty across tasks, which shifts the RT distribution for harder tasks later in time.
Consequently, the optimal policy is consistent with the shortest processing time first algorithm.
We conducted a study in which observers were presented with 4 dynamic RDKs and asked to select them in order of easiest to hardest.
Unlike the other experiments in this paper, there was no requirement to make an RDK judgment after selection.
The untimed and deadline phases were kept the same as in Experiment 2; however, removing task completions left ample time to select all four tasks.
Hence, the results from this experiment provide an indication of how accurately difficulty can be judged with limited time pressure.
Only the random location condition was investigated.
A selection only experiment also permits two further independent analyses.
First, we assess the selection RTs to motivate the observation windows used in Experiment 3.
Second, we measure the precision with which observers can discriminate coherence levels by fitting a Thurstonian confusion model to the selection choices (Thurstone, 1927).
text.formatted: Second, we measure the precision with which observers can discriminate coherence levels by fitting a Thurstonian confusion model to the selection choices <ref type="bibr" target="#b122">(Thurstone, 1927)</ref>.

text.text: With four tasks, each selection order implies a set of six paired comparison judgments (e.g., easy vs medium, easy vs hard, medium vs hard, hard vs very hard, etc).
The probability of selecting the easier task given the difference in coherence is a psychometric function of difficulty discrimination.
The slope of this function is an estimate of observation precision.

Once established, the parameters of the Thurstonian model can be fixed and used to, for example, estimate effect sizes for power analysis and estimate observation precision as a test of our hypothesis in Experiment 3.

text.text: Sixty-one participants from the University of Melbourne were recruited through the undergraduate Research Experience Program and received subject credit in return for participation.

Datasets from 9 subjects were excluded for completing fewer than 20 deadline trials for completing the experiment more than once (i.e., only the first of the datasets for these subjects was retained) leaving 52 participants (43 Female, 9 Male, 1 Unspecified, age range 17-36).

The experiment was programmed in HTML and Javascript using the jsPsych package 4, entropy decreases across blocks in both conditions but more so in the Fixed location condition compared to the Random Location condition indicating that selection orders became more stable across the course of the experiment in the Fixed Location condition.
The Random condition never reached the same level of stability as the Fixed Location condition.

We analyzed entropy using a multilevel regression with condition, block (as a linear trend centred on the middle of the experiment), and their interaction as predictors, and a random intercept and block slope for each participant.
At the midpoint, entropy was 3.39 bits higher in the Random Location condition, 95% CI [2.97, 3.82], R² β = .52.
Entropy decreased by 0.25 bits per block in the Fixed Location condition, 95% CI [-0.34, -0.16], and by 0.11 bits per block in the Random Location condition, 95% CI [-0.20, -0.03] .
Eighty-six participants were recruited in total (Bracketed (200|400|800) Condition N = 42, Anchored (400|800|1600) Condition N = 44).

Several participants were removed for completing less than 20 trials at any observation window leaving N = 34 in the Bracketed condition (29 F, 5 M; mean age 19, range 18-22) and N = 39 in the Anchored condition (32 F, 6 M, 1 Unspecified; mean age 19, range 18-24).
Participants were recruited from the Melbourne Research Experience Program and were reimbursed with credit toward an undergraduate psychology subject.
All participants completed the experiment in their own browser using an experiment programmed with JSPsych (De Leeuw, 2015).
